# Hypertension prevalence and the treatment gap

NFHS-5, conducted across 2019-21, puts age-standardised hypertension prevalence
among Indian adults at **22.4 per cent** (21.3 per cent in women, 24.0 per cent
in men). The Indian Council of Medical Research's National Non-communicable
Disease Monitoring Survey (2017-18), which covers a wider 18-69 age band, puts
it higher at **28.5 per cent**.

The number that matters commercially is not prevalence but the treatment
cascade. In NFHS-5, only **40.7 per cent of previously diagnosed cases were on
blood-pressure-lowering medication**. Prevalence is high; penetration is low.

State-level variation is wide - from roughly 15-18 per cent in Rajasthan and
Ladakh to 34-42 per cent in Sikkim and 31-38 per cent in Punjab - which means
national averages understate the concentration of opportunity in specific
geographies.

## Why this matters for prioritisation

The anti-hypertensive market is not a mature, saturated category being defended
on price. It is a category where the majority of diagnosed patients are still
not on therapy, which supports volume-led rather than price-led growth over a
three-to-five-year horizon. This is a broad tailwind across the
anti-hypertensive segment; it does not by itself favour any one molecule class,
so it is applied at segment level.
